title: Direct mass measurements of the high-spin isomers in self-conjugate 94Ag
summary: Two decades ago, two-proton emission from a $(21^+)$ isomeric state in $^{94}$Ag was reported. This report has remained the sole example of possible two-proton radioactivity in a nucleus with an odd number of protons on the chart of nuclei. A debate regarding the viability of the decay mode has been ongoing due to the unknown mass of the isomer. Here, using state-selective laser ionization in a hot cavity catcher, we present multi-reflection time-of-flight mass spectrometry of the long-lived isomeric states of $^{94}$Ag and its one-proton decay daughter $^{93}$Pd. For the first time, direct mass measurements of the $(7^+)$ and $(21^+)$ isomeric states set the stage for an independent discussion of the energetics of these decays. We rule out the two-proton emission from the $(21^+)$ state as previously reported and reveal the one-proton decay energy to be significantly lower. State-of-the-art shell-model calculations reproduce the energy gap of the $(7^+)$ and the $(21^+)$ states as well as the half-life of the $(21^+)$ state, implying the $(21^+)$ state is likely near-spherical, contradicting the reported explanation for the two-proton radioactivity. Importantly, the techniques employed are a stepping stone towards the first laser spectroscopic investigation of a proton-emitting state

title: Nuclear Modification of $π^0$ Production in pO and OO Collisions with ALICE
comment: Contribution to the proceedings for the 13th International Conference on Hard and Electromagnetic Probes of High-Energy Nuclear Collisions (Hard Probes 2026)
summary:
Energy loss of high-momentum partons is one of the key signatures of the quark--gluon plasma formed in heavy-ion collisions. Through measurements of the nuclear modification factor, $R_{\rm AA}$, where a strong suppression of high-$p_{\rm T}$ particle yields is observed, parton energy loss has been confirmed in Pb--Pb collisions at the LHC. However, in small collision systems, like pp and p--Pb, energy loss has not yet been confirmed.
  In this contribution, a measurement of the $π^0$ $R_{\rm AA}$ in OO and pO collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.36$ TeV and $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 9.62$ TeV, respectively, is presented. These results are based on the measured $π^0$ $p_{\rm T}$ spectra in OO, pO, and pp collisions using the ALICE electromagnetic calorimeter. The measurement of the $R_{\rm pO}$ allows for precise constraints on cold-nuclear matter effects. In combination with the $R_{\rm OO}$, this allows for a separation of cold and hot nuclear matter contributions and enables a quantitative determination of partonic energy loss in OO collisions. The measurements are compared to theoretical model calculations that include both cold and hot nuclear matter effects.

title: Anatomy of charge radii of Ca nuclei in self-consistent approaches with Skyrme and Fayans functionals
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures; to be published in JPS Conf. Proc. (ARIS2026)
summary: It has been known that the $^{40-48}$Ca nuclei have anomalous $N$-dependence of their charge radii. While difficult to reproduce in most self-consistent calculations, the parabolic behavior in $^{42,44,46}$Ca is reproduced with the Fayans functional, although it tends to overestimate the charge radii at the neutron-deficient $^{38}$Ca. We investigate the origin of the $N$-dependence with the Fayans functional by decomposing it into radial contributions, and trace it back to the single-particle potentials and neutron pair densities. The results are compared with those of a Skyrme functional SkM$^\ast$, which is considered a representative of the usual functionals. It is found that, in the results of the Fayans functional, the origin is shared between the parabolic behavior in $^{42,44,46}$Ca and the erroneous enhancement of the charge radii at $^{38}$Ca. To fully resolve the puzzle with respect to the parabolic charge radii in $^{42,44,46}$Ca, it is vital to reproduce the neutron-deficient region simultaneously.

title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Total Kinetic Energy Distributions in Neutron-Induced Fission
summary: The incident-neutron-energy dependence of post-neutron total-kinetic-energy (TKE) distributions, particularly their width in the multichance-fission regime, provides a sensitive test of fission calculations. We investigate how the General Description of Fission Observables (GEF) and probabilistic machine-learning models trained on GEF reproduce measured TKE distributions, emphasizing their width at high incident-neutron energies and extrapolation beyond the training range. Gaussian process regression (GPR), GPR with a white-noise kernel, a mixture density network (MDN), and a Bayesian mixture density network (BMDN) are evaluated on a common calculated dataset. An extended MDN/BMDN analysis uses 1,025 GEF spectra from 20 target nuclei and 60 measured distributions. Training ranges of up to 20, 40, and approximately 76 MeV are compared with matched-size controls extending to 30 or 40 MeV while preserving the number of spectra per target. Above 40 MeV, the BMDN width mean absolute error relative to experiment decreases from 5.63 MeV for training up to 20 MeV to 2.70 and 2.53 MeV for two matched-size 30-MeV controls and 1.77 MeV for the matched-size 40-MeV control. Predictive-interval coverage relative to GEF above 40 MeV rises from 52.3% to 92.3% between the 20-MeV and full training ranges. Agreement with measured mean TKE and widths is target dependent, with no uniform ordering among GEF, MDN, and BMDN. The results demonstrate the sensitivity of high-energy widths to training-energy coverage, with improvements already evident at 30 MeV. The comparatively slow variation of GEF widths at high energies limits the extent to which these improvements can be attributed to learning nontrivial energy dependence. Adequate training-energy coverage is critical for reproducing the calculated high-energy evolution, while agreement with experiment remains constrained by the underlying fission model.

title: Introducing Parton-Level Fluctuations in the TRENTo-Sea Model
summary: A variety of experimental and theoretical data suggest that initial condition models for heavy-ion collisions contain a degree of sub-nucleonic fluctuations. While current models fit the number and size of these fluctuations to data, we use nuclear parton distribution functions to constrain sub-nucleonic structure and fluctuations in TRENTo-Sea, an extension of TRENTo. Sampling the momentum fraction distributions of quarks and gluons in heavy ions, we use perturbative quantum chromodynamics to collide nuclei at the parton level, and we introduce an infrared center-of-momentum damping scale which is tuned to proton-proton cross sections. We find that our model successfully reproduces the $\varepsilon_2\{2\}$ of data-calibrated models except in central collisions, and an analysis of the power spectrum and granularity of the pre-equilibrium fireball shows that the number of low-$x$ partons in a nucleon has a significant effect on the local transverse geometry. Our model is largely insensitive to variations of the infrared parameters, as such changes are absorbed into the calibration of the infrared regulator. We expect that this work will aid future research on soft-hard correlations and constraining different nPDF sets.

title: Large-scale fission properties with BSkG3 I : fission paths and spontaneous fission half-lives
summary: We present our first large-scale analysis of nuclear fission properties based on the BSkG3 energy density functional. Building on the model's unprecedented agreement with ground state observables and fission data in the actinide region, we survey nearly 3300 nuclei with $80\leq Z\leq118$, spanning the region between the predicted proton and neutron drip lines. We calculate thousands of potential energy surfaces that explicitly account for triaxial and octupole deformations. We determine the corresponding least-action fission paths using microscopic collective inertias derived consistently from BSkG3 and calculate spontaneous fission (SF) half-lives within the semiclassical WKB approximation. Our results reveal a rich diversity of fission path topologies, extending well beyond the conventional two-humped picture commonly adopted in reaction codes, and a wide variety of nuclear shapes along these paths, highlighting the limitations of exploring only one collective degree of freedom. In particular, triaxiality affects not only inner barriers in the actinide region but also outer barriers and single barriers in several regions of the superheavy nuclei. Our predicted SF half-lives follow trends similar to those of previous large-scale studies, although significant differences emerge near the neutron drip line. The resulting dataset, including fission barriers, SF half-lives, and saddle-point nuclear level densities, is available has been incorporated into the TALYS reaction code and the BRUSLIB repository. It provides a microscopic foundation for nuclear reaction calculations and astrophysical applications, particularly rapid neutron-capture simulations, which require reliable fission properties of nuclei far from the valley of stability.

title: Equilibrium baseline for transverse-momentum correlations in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 3$-$39$ GeV: Conservation laws, resonance decays, quantum statistics, and collective flow
summary: Event-by-event transverse-momentum correlations measured by STAR in Au+Au collisions exhibit a nonmonotonic energy dependence with a minimum near $\sqrt{s_{NN}} \approx 5$-$8$ GeV and a steep rise toward $3$ GeV. Before interpreting these features in terms of a softened equation of state or a QCD critical point, the baseline from an equilibrated hadron resonance gas must be established. Here we compute the two-particle correlator $\langle Δp_{T,i}Δp_{T,j} \rangle$ in thermal and chemical equilibrium from $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 3$ to $39$ GeV for 0-5% and 30-40% collisions, incorporating resonance decays, Bose-Einstein statistics, Bjorken longitudinal and transverse radial flow, and global conservation of energy, baryon number, electric charge, strangeness, and transverse momentum. Imposing conservation laws via a saddle-point expansion of the microcanonical ensemble yields the variance of any additive observable as a Schur complement of grand-canonical covariances. Although the equilibrium gas undergoes the transition from baryon- to meson-dominated matter, composition fluctuations cancel the large negative "mixing" term that arises when species multiplicities are fixed event by event, leaving only a much smaller negative conservation residual. Across $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 11.5$-$39$ GeV, the equilibrium baseline with strong flow underpredicts the data by a factor of $3$-$4$ in 0-5% and $\approx 6.5$ in 30-40% collisions; at fixed-target energies ($3$-$5.2$ GeV), where the data are largest and positive, the baseline turns negative. Accounting for the data via radial-flow fluctuations at fixed energy requires $σ_β/β_s \approx 6$-$10\%$ in central and $\approx 22\%$ in 30-40% collider-energy collisions, growing faster with decreasing centrality than independent-source scaling.

title: Microscopic Approach to Neutron Elastic and Inelastic Cross Sections
summary: Depending on the nuclei involved and the beam energies, reaction timescales differ tremendously. Today, distinct models are often used to describe each timescale, relying on phenomenological inputs, such as level densities or partial-widths, which limits their predictive power. This work aims to address this issue by providing a unified description of low-energy neutron elastic and inelastic reaction channels starting from microscopic predictions of the structure of mid-mass nuclei. The goal is to build a framework that is general enough to span the different reaction regimes while remaining anchored in microscopic theory. For illustration purposes, this work focuses on reactions $n+^{20}$Ne to the elastic and inelastic channels. The S-matrix is build from shell model predictions of resonances states and their spectroscopic amplitudes for $^{21}$Ne, using two different approximations of the single-particle asymptotics. Then, the shell-model predictions for the level density and single-particle partial widths are analyzed and the final cross sections are compared with evaluated ones. This method qualitatively reproduces the ENDF evaluation for the $^{20}$Ne$(n,el)$ and $^{20}$Ne$(n,n')$ cross sections. The present study also compares the Shannon entropy obtained from this model to the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE). In the future, the framework will be extended to include more complex reaction channels, such as two-nucleon and gamma channels, enabling more accurate predictions of neutron-induced reactions such as those of astrophysical interest.
